title: CLI args / flags
summary: Parse command-line arguments and flags in each language.
when_to_use: Building CLIs, tools, and scripts that take options and positional args.

c.notes: Raw argv; use getopt/getopt_long on Linux or parse manually on Windows.

python.code:
import argparse

p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="demo")
p.add_argument("path")
p.add_argument("-n", "--name", default="world")
p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
args = p.parse_args()
print(args.path, args.name, args.verbose)

pitfalls: Don't assume argv[0] is the program path on all platforms.
Quote-aware shell splitting differs from language argv parsing.

title: File read/write (text + bytes)
summary: Read and write text and binary files with idiomatic APIs.
when_to_use: Config, logs, assets, or any disk I/O.

c.notes: fopen modes: rb/wb for bytes; text is platform-dependent.

rust.notes: std::fs for whole-file; BufReader/Writer for streams.

python.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("hello.txt")
p.write_text("hi\n", encoding="utf-8")
text = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
p.write_bytes(b"\x00\x01")
data = p.read_bytes()
print(text, data)
python.notes: pathlib preferred over open() for simple cases.

pitfalls: Always specify encoding for text (UTF-8) on Windows Python.
C text mode translates newlines on Windows — use binary for exact bytes.

title: JSON encode/decode
summary: Serialize and parse JSON objects.
when_to_use: APIs, config files, inter-process data exchange.

c.notes: N/A in ISO C — pick cJSON, jansson, or similar.

python.code:
import json

obj = {"name": "a", "count": 2}
s = json.dumps(obj)
back = json.loads(s)
print(s, back)

pitfalls: C: no standard library JSON — document the dependency.
Numbers: JSON numbers are doubles; prefer integers carefully across langs.

title: HTTP client GET/POST
summary: Minimal HTTP GET and POST from a client.
when_to_use: Calling REST APIs or fetching remote resources.

c.notes: N/A in ISO C — use libcurl or WinHTTP on Windows.

go.notes: net/http Client; prefer context timeouts in real code.

rust.notes: req (guide name for the HTTP client; async or blocking).

python.code:
# stdlib:
from urllib.request import urlopen, Request
print(urlopen("https://example.com/").read()[:80])

# or requests (third-party):
# import requests
# r = requests.post("https://httpbin.org/post", json={"ok": True})
# print(r.status_code, r.json())
python.notes: urllib for stdlib; requests is popular.

pitfalls: Always set timeouts; hung connections are common.
TLS trust store / proxy env vars differ per platform.
Cargo.toml dependency key remains reqwest on crates.io; this guide calls it req.

title: Error handling idioms
summary: Idiomatic ways to report and propagate failures.
when_to_use: Any non-trivial function that can fail.

c.notes: Return codes + errno; check every call.

go.notes: error as last return value; wrap with fmt.Errorf %w.

python.notes: Exceptions; prefer specific types over bare Exception.

pitfalls: Swallowing errors silently hides bugs.
In Go, never ignore err with `_` unless intentional.

title: Strings / UTF-8 / bytes
summary: Work with Unicode text vs raw byte sequences.
when_to_use: Parsing text, paths, network payloads, or mixed encodings.

c.notes: C char* is bytes; encoding is convention.

go.notes: string is UTF-8 immutable bytes; range yields runes.

rust.notes: String vs &[u8] / Vec<u8>; OsString for paths.

python.code:
s = "café"
b = s.encode("utf-8")
back = b.decode("utf-8")
print(len(s), len(b), back)
# bytes vs str: never mix without encode/decode
python.notes: str is Unicode; bytes is raw.

pitfalls: len()/strlen count bytes, not grapheme clusters.
Windows APIs often use UTF-16 (wchar_t / WCHAR).

title: Environment variables
summary: Read and set process environment variables.
when_to_use: Config, secrets injection (carefully), path overrides.

c.notes: getenv; HOME vs USERPROFILE.

python.code:
import os

print(os.environ.get("PATH", ""))
os.environ["MY_FLAG"] = "1"
print(os.environ["MY_FLAG"])

pitfalls: Don't log secrets from the environment.
Child processes inherit env — sanitize when spawning.

title: Path join / exist / mkdir
summary: Join path segments, check existence, create directories.
when_to_use: Portable filesystem layout across Windows and Linux.

c.notes: No portable join in C — use snprintf with / or \ carefully.

go.notes: path/filepath is OS-aware; path is slash-only.

python.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("a") / "b" / "c.txt"
p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print(p, p.exists())

pitfalls: Never join with string + on Windows (wrong separators).
Check trailing separators and empty segments.

title: Subprocess / exec
summary: Spawn a child process and capture output.
when_to_use: Calling other tools, pipelines, or wrappers.

c.notes: system() is simple but limited; prefer CreateProcess / posix_spawn.

python.code:
import subprocess

r = subprocess.run(["echo", "hello"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
print(r.stdout)
# avoid shell=True unless you must

pitfalls: shell=True / system() invite injection if args are untrusted.
PATH lookup and .exe extension differ on Windows.

title: Threads / async / concurrency basics
summary: Minimal concurrent work: threads, goroutines, async tasks.
when_to_use: Overlapping I/O or CPU work; start simple.

c.notes: C11 threads.h, pthreads, or CreateThread.

go.notes: go keyword + WaitGroup; channels for messaging.

python.code:
import threading
import asyncio

def work():
    print("thread")

t = threading.Thread(target=work)
t.start(); t.join()

async def main():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    print("async")

asyncio.run(main())
python.notes: threading for OS threads; asyncio for concurrent I/O.

pitfalls: Shared mutable state needs synchronization.
Python GIL limits CPU parallelism in threads — use multiprocessing for CPU.

title: Mutex / sync primitives (high level)
summary: Protect shared state with locks / mutexes.
when_to_use: When multiple threads mutate the same data.

c.notes: pthread_mutex or CRITICAL_SECTION on Windows.

go.code:
package main

import "sync"

func main() {
    var mu sync.Mutex
    var n int
    mu.Lock()
    n++
    mu.Unlock()
    _ = n
    // Prefer channels when they fit; sync.Mutex when they don't
}

python.code:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
n = 0
with lock:
    n += 1
print(n)

pitfalls: Deadlocks from lock ordering — always acquire in a consistent order.
Hold locks for as short a time as possible.

title: TCP listen + connect (minimal)
summary: Minimal TCP server listen and client connect.
when_to_use: Custom protocols, health checks, local tooling.

c.notes: POSIX sockets vs Winsock (WSAStartup required).

python.code:
import socket
import threading

def server():
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9000))
        s.listen(1)
        c, _ = s.accept()
        with c:
            print("srv", c.recv(16))

threading.Thread(target=server, daemon=True).start()
with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 9000)) as c:
    c.sendall(b"ping")

pitfalls: Always handle partial reads/writes.
SO_REUSEADDR behavior differs slightly on Windows.

title: Timers / sleep / deadlines
summary: Sleep, timers, and operation deadlines.
when_to_use: Retries, rate limits, canceling stuck I/O.

c.code:
#ifdef _WIN32
#include <windows.h>
Sleep(100); /* milliseconds */
#else
#include <unistd.h>
usleep(100 * 1000); /* or nanosleep */
#endif
c.notes: Sleep / usleep / nanosleep.

python.code:
import time
import asyncio

time.sleep(0.1)

async def main():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

asyncio.run(main())

pitfalls: Busy-wait loops waste CPU — prefer sleep/event waits.
Always propagate cancellation/deadlines through I/O stacks.

title: Logging basics
summary: Emit structured or leveled log messages.
when_to_use: Diagnostics, ops, and debugging without printf soup.

c.notes: No std log API — macros to stderr are common.

python.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(levelname)s %(message)s",
)
logging.info("ready count=%s", 3)
logging.warning("careful")

pitfalls: Don't log secrets or full PII.
Prefer structured fields over string concatenation.

title: Maps / dicts / hash maps
summary: Key-value collections: insert, lookup, iterate.
when_to_use: Indexes, caches, frequency counts, config tables.

c.code:
/* No stdlib hashmap in C. Options:
   - uthash macros
   - GLib GHashTable
   - roll your own open addressing
*/
c.notes: N/A in ISO C — use a library.

pitfalls: Go: concurrent map writes panic — use sync.Map or a mutex.
Hash iteration order is randomized in Go and Python 3.7+ insertion-ordered for dict.

title: Sorting / searching a list
summary: Sort a slice/list and binary-search it.
when_to_use: Ordered views, lookups, top-N.

c.notes: qsort / bsearch in stdlib.

python.code:
a = [3, 1, 2]
a.sort()
import bisect
i = bisect.bisect_left(a, 2)
print(a, i, a[i] if i < len(a) and a[i] == 2 else None)

pitfalls: bsearch/BinarySearch require a sorted collection.
Unstable vs stable sort matters when keys tie.

title: Regex match
summary: Match and capture with regular expressions.
when_to_use: Validation, light parsing, log scraping.

c.notes: POSIX regex.h on Linux; use PCRE2 or C++ on Windows.

python.code:
import re

m = re.match(r"^(\w+)@(\w+)$", "a@b")
if m:
    print(m.group(1), m.group(2))

pitfalls: Catastrophic backtracking — prefer RE2-style engines for untrusted input.
Compile once; reuse the pattern object.

title: Date/time formatting
summary: Format timestamps for logs and APIs.
when_to_use: Logs, filenames, HTTP headers, user display.

c.notes: strftime; prefer UTC for logs.

go.notes: Reference time layout: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006.

rust.notes: chrono or time crate; std has limited formatting.

python.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
print(now.isoformat())
print(now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"))

pitfalls: Naive local time without zone offsets causes bugs across DST.
Go's layout uses a fixed reference date, not strftime tokens.

title: Unit test skeleton
summary: Minimal unit-test layout for each language.
when_to_use: Locking in behavior as you add features.

c.notes: assert for tiny tests; Unity/Check/CTest for suites.

python.code:
# test_add.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5

# pytest test_add.py
# or: python -m unittest

pitfalls: Keep tests deterministic — no real network/clock without fakes.
Name tests after behavior, not implementation details.

title: Module / package layout (hello project)
summary: Minimal project layout and how to import your own code.
when_to_use: Starting a new tool or library the idiomatic way.

c.notes: Headers + sources; CMake or Make for builds.

python.code:
# pyproject.toml or:
# hello/
#   __init__.py
#   greet.py
# main.py

# greet.py
def greet():
    return "hi"

# main.py
from hello.greet import greet
print(greet())
# pip install -e .  or PYTHONPATH=.

pitfalls: Circular imports — keep dependency edges one-way.
Don't put secrets in the repo; use env or local config.

title: Lists / slices / vecs
summary: Growable sequences: append, index, and length.
when_to_use: Ordered collections that change size at runtime.

c.notes: N/A in ISO C — implement or use a library (GArray, stb stretchy).

go.notes: slices are views over arrays; append may reallocate.

rust.notes: Vec<T> owns; &[T] borrows a contiguous view.

python.code:
xs = [1, 2]
xs.append(3)
print(xs[0], len(xs))
xs.extend([4, 5])
print(xs[1:3])  # slice copy
python.notes: list is the growable sequence; slicing copies.

pitfalls: Go: append may move the backing array — never keep stale pointers into it.
Rust: indexing panics on OOB; prefer get() when unsure.
C: forgetting to free or double-free after realloc.

title: Iteration / for-each / range
summary: Idiomatic ways to walk collections and sequences.
when_to_use: Any time you process every element (or an index range).

c.notes: Index loops; no language-level for-each over collections.

go.notes: range over slices, maps, strings, channels.

python.notes: for-in over any iterable; enumerate for index.

pitfalls: Go: ranging a map yields random order.
Mutating a collection while iterating often invalidates iterators (Rust borrow checker; Python RuntimeError).
C: sizeof(array) only works on real arrays, not decayed pointers.

title: Types / structs / methods
summary: Define a composite type and attach behavior (methods).
when_to_use: Modeling domain data with operations that belong on it.

c.notes: No methods — use functions taking struct pointers.

go.notes: methods with value or pointer receivers.

python.notes: classes; dataclasses for plain data + methods.

pitfalls: Go: value receivers copy; use pointer receivers to mutate.
Rust: cannot mutably borrow while also immutably borrowing the same field path.
C: passing structs by value copies — prefer const pointers for large types.

title: Optionals / null / Result
summary: Represent absence and recoverable failure without silent null crashes.
when_to_use: Lookups that may miss, parse that may fail, or nullable fields.

c.notes: N/A Option/Result types — use NULL, sentinels, or return codes.

go.notes: comma-ok for maps/lookups; error for failures (see error-handling).

rust.notes: Option<T> for absence; Result<T,E> for errors; ? to propagate.

python.notes: None for absence; exceptions (or Result libs) for errors.

pitfalls: Dereferencing NULL / None / unwrap causes crashes — check first.
Go: zero value is valid data — prefer comma-ok or pointers when zero is ambiguous.
Rust: unwrap() in library code is usually wrong; prefer ? or expect with context.

title: String formatting
summary: Build strings with printf-style, format!, f-strings, or fmt.
when_to_use: Logs, UI text, filenames, and debug dumps.

c.notes: snprintf — always pass the buffer size.

go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    n := 42
    s := fmt.Sprintf("n=%d hex=%#x", n, n)
    fmt.Println(s)
}

python.code:
n = 42
s = f"n={n} hex={n:#x}"
print(s)
print("{n} {n:#x}".format(n=n))

pitfalls: C: sprintf without bounds is buffer-overflow territory — use snprintf.
Never pass untrusted strings as the format string (format-string attacks).
Locale can change decimal separators for floating formats.

title: Hashing + Base64
summary: SHA-256 digest and Base64 encode/decode with stdlib or one common lib.
when_to_use: Checksums, content IDs, and binary-safe text transport.

c.notes: N/A in ISO C — use OpenSSL, mbedtls, or similar.

rust.notes: sha2 + base64 crates (no crypto hash in std).

python.code:
import base64
import hashlib

sum_ = hashlib.sha256(b"hi").digest()
enc = base64.b64encode(sum_).decode()
raw = base64.b64decode(enc)
print(sum_.hex(), enc, raw.hex())

pitfalls: SHA-256 is not encryption and not a password KDF — use Argon2/bcrypt for passwords.
Base64 is not URL-safe by default — use URLEncoding / urlsafe_b64* when needed.
Always compare digests in constant time when used as auth tokens.

title: CSV / line-oriented parsing
summary: Read CSV rows or simple line-oriented records.
when_to_use: Logs, exports, and tabular text from other tools.

c.notes: strtok is naive — no quoted fields; prefer a CSV library for real data.

rust.notes: csv crate; for lines only use BufRead::lines.

python.code:
import csv
from io import StringIO

text = "a,b\n1,2\n"
for row in csv.reader(StringIO(text)):
    print(row)

# line-oriented:
for line in text.splitlines():
    print(line.split(","))
python.notes: csv stdlib; splitlines for plain line parse.

pitfalls: Naive split on commas breaks on quoted commas and embedded newlines.
Always decide encoding (UTF-8) and newline style (CRLF on Windows).
strtok modifies the buffer and is not thread-safe.

title: Build / deps basics
summary: One-liner project init and how to add a dependency.
when_to_use: Starting a project or pulling in a library.

c.code:
# Minimal Makefile
# CC=cc CFLAGS=-Wall -O2
# hello: hello.c
# 	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $< -lm
#
# CMake one-shot:
#   cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
# CMakeLists.txt:
#   cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
#   project(hello C)
#   add_executable(hello hello.c)
#   # find_package / FetchContent for deps
c.notes: Makefile or CMake; deps via pkg-config, FetchContent, or vendoring.

go.code:
# go mod init example.com/hello
# go get golang.org/x/text@latest
# go run .
go.notes: go mod init + go get; go.sum locks versions.

rust.code:
# cargo new hello && cd hello
# cargo add serde --features derive
# cargo build / cargo run
rust.notes: cargo new + cargo add (or edit Cargo.toml).

python.code:
# pip install requests
# or: uv init && uv add requests
# or pyproject.toml + pip install -e .

pitfalls: Pin or lock deps for reproducible builds (go.sum, Cargo.lock, uv.lock).
Don't commit secrets or local absolute paths in build files.
C: mismatched ABI / missing -l flags cause link errors that look like missing headers.

title: Graceful shutdown / signals
summary: Handle Ctrl-C / SIGINT and shut down cleanly on Windows and Linux.
when_to_use: Servers, long jobs, and CLIs that must flush or close resources.

c.notes: POSIX: sigaction(SIGINT). Windows: signal(SIGINT) or SetConsoleCtrlHandler.

go.code:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
)

func main() {
    ch := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
    signal.Notify(ch, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
    fmt.Println("running; Ctrl-C to stop")
    <-ch
    fmt.Println("bye")
}
go.notes: os/signal; Interrupt is Ctrl-C on both platforms.

rust.notes: ctrlc crate covers Unix signals + Windows console ctrl.

python.code:
import signal
import sys

stop = False

def on_int(signum, frame):
    global stop
    stop = True

signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, on_int)
# Linux also: signal.SIGTERM; Windows limited signal set
print("running; Ctrl-C to stop")
while not stop:
    pass
print("bye")
sys.exit(0)
python.notes: signal.SIGINT works on Win+Linux; SIGTERM mainly Unix.

pitfalls: Async-signal-unsafe: only set a flag in the handler; do real cleanup in the main loop.
Windows has a smaller signal set — prefer console ctrl handlers / language wrappers.
Ignoring SIGPIPE on servers can hide broken-client bugs — know your defaults.

title: SQLite basics
summary: Open a SQLite database and run a simple query.
when_to_use: Local persistence, caches, and embedded apps.

c.notes: sqlite3 C API — not ISO C stdlib; system or amalgamated lib.

go.notes: database/sql + modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go) or mattn CGO driver.

python.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t(x)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES(1)")
print(con.execute("SELECT x FROM t").fetchone()[0])
con.close()
python.notes: sqlite3 is in the Python stdlib.

pitfalls: Always use parameterized queries — never string-format SQL with user input.
Check every prepare/step/exec return code; SQLite errors are easy to ignore.
WAL mode and concurrent writers need awareness on multi-process apps.

title: Windows paths + CreateProcess
summary: Win32 path quirks and CreateProcess vs Unix exec.
when_to_use: Spawning processes or building paths correctly on Windows.

c.notes: CreateProcessW vs Unix fork/exec/posix_spawn; cmdline is a mutable string.

go.notes: path/filepath + os/exec; Go wraps CreateProcess on Windows.

python.code:
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess

p = Path("C:/Temp") / "a" / "b.txt"
print(p)
r = subprocess.run(["cmd", "/c", "echo", "hello"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
print(r.stdout)
python.notes: pathlib accepts /; subprocess list form avoids shell quoting issues.

pitfalls: CreateProcess requires a writable command-line buffer; string literals crash.
MAX_PATH (260) still bites without long-path opt-in or \\?\ prefix.
Forward vs backslash and case-insensitivity differ from Unix — don't hard-code style.

title: Linux permissions / umask
summary: File mode bits, chmod, and umask basics on Linux.
when_to_use: Creating files/dirs with the right access mode on Unix.

c.notes: open mode is masked by umask; chmod sets absolute mode.

go.notes: os.WriteFile / os.Chmod; umask via syscall or shell.

rust.notes: PermissionsExt on Unix; mode still subject to umask on create.

python.code:
import os

old = os.umask(0o022)
try:
    fd = os.open("secret.txt", os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY | os.O_TRUNC, 0o600)
    os.write(fd, b"x")
    os.close(fd)
    os.chmod("secret.txt", 0o640)
finally:
    os.umask(old)
python.notes: os.umask / os.chmod / os.open; pathlib also supports chmod.

pitfalls: Requested create mode is AND-masked with ~umask — 0o666 with umask 022 becomes 0o644.
chmod follows symlinks' targets on some APIs — know lchmod vs chmod.
Windows ACLs are a different model — these APIs are Unix-oriented.
